name: Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren)
lead: Aminoglutethimide is an oral nonsteroidal glutarimide, sold under names including Cytadren, Elipten and Orimeten. It was introduced in 1960 as an anticonvulsant, then found to inhibit steroid synthesis, and was later used for Cushing's syndrome, postmenopausal breast cancer and prostate cancer.[1] It was among the first adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors and the first aromatase inhibitor used clinically.[1][2]

For physique purposes, the route people describe runs through two hormones: lowering cortisol (which is catabolic) to protect muscle while dieting, and blocking aromatase to limit estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia, water retention and fat gain from anabolic steroids. Wikipedia notes that its usefulness for these purposes has been questioned, that few users report positive experiences and that its risks are considered high.[1] No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.[3]

Online it is usually called Cytadren. It turns up in 2000s-era T Nation threads on estrogen control and contest-prep cycles, often next to anastrozole (Arimidex), and in speculation about the deaths of professional bodybuilders.[10][11][12]

Aminoglutethimide is prescription-only where it is sold and has been discontinued in the US and EU; it remains available as generic tablets in a few markets such as China, Egypt and Lithuania [1][9]. Because its use for physique goals relies on pharmacology and forum report rather than trials, the sections below separate what the medical literature shows from what bodybuilding communities say.

chain: Blocks adrenal steroid production and aromatase
Lower cortisol and less estrogen conversion
Claimed: less muscle loss while dieting and fewer estrogenic side effects on anabolic cycles
angle.text: Bodybuilders have used aminoglutethimide to try to cut cortisol and control estrogen while dieting or on anabolic steroids, with the aim of holding muscle and looking leaner. These effects come from its pharmacology and user reports and have not been measured in appearance trials.

infobox: Prescription drug where marketed; marketed in few countries [1]
Nonsteroidal glutarimide, derivative of glutethimide; C13H16N2O2, about 232 g/mol [1]

paras: Uses include epilepsy (petit mal), Cushing's syndrome, hormone-sensitive breast cancer in postmenopausal women and prostate cancer. It is given with a corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone to prevent adrenal insufficiency, is a second- or third-line option in breast cancer and is not effective in premenopausal women.[1] Ketoconazole produces similar hormone reductions and is described as moderately less toxic.[1]

Bodybuilders and other men have used it to lower cortisol, which is catabolic, and to inhibit aromatase to reduce effects such as gynecomastia, water retention and fat gain from anabolic steroids, often alongside an anabolic steroid to avoid androgen deficiency.[1]

Forum posters describe it as an alternative to anastrozole for estrogen control and as a cortisol suppressor during contest preparation; others say it is rarely worth the lethargy it causes, and one notes that a trial showing an estrogen effect also gave hydrocortisone, which has independent benefits.[10][13][14]

Aminoglutethimide is a reversible, nonselective competitive inhibitor of several steroidogenic enzymes, including aromatase, the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme P450scc, 21-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase and aldosterone synthase. Blocking P450scc suppresses adrenal steroid production, sometimes called a reversible chemical adrenalectomy. It is reported to reduce aromatase activity by 74 to 92 percent and lower estradiol by 58 to 76 percent in men and postmenopausal women, though it is considered a relatively weak aromatase inhibitor.[1] A 1978 study reported that it inhibited extraglandular estrogen production in postmenopausal women with breast cancer, and a 1967 study examined its mechanism in blocking adrenal corticosteroid synthesis.[4][5]

Oral absorption is rapid and complete, and the half-life is about 12.5 hours after a single dose; about a third to a half is excreted unchanged in urine [1]. Grokipedia adds that the half-life shortens to about 7 hours with chronic use because the drug induces liver enzymes [9]. Wikipedia lists related compounds that include rogletimide, metyrapone and mitotane [1]. It is described as having antiestrogenic, antiandrogenic, antiglucocorticoid and antimineralocorticoid effects because it reduces several hormone classes at once [1].

Introduced in 1960 as an anticonvulsant, it was reported in 1963 to cause Addison-like symptoms in a young girl, a serendipitous finding that revealed steroid-synthesis inhibition. It was withdrawn in 1966 because of adverse effects, then reported in breast cancer in 1969 and prostate cancer in 1974.[1] Third-generation drugs such as letrozole were compared against it in trials.[6]

Wikipedia gives the developmental code name Ciba 16038, and its brand names include Elipten, Cytadren and Orimeten.[1] A 1978 report that the drug inhibits extraglandular estrogen production in postmenopausal women with breast cancer, and histories of aromatase research, place it as the first aromatase inhibitor used in breast cancer, later followed by drugs such as vorozole, anastrozole and letrozole.[2][4][6] An AI-generated overview reports that the Cytadren brand was approved by the FDA for Cushing's syndrome in 1980 and later discontinued in major markets, a statement not confirmed in the other sources.[9]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, states that Ciba synthesised the compound in 1958 as an analog of glutethimide, that studies in 1967 showed it inhibited adrenal corticosteroid synthesis, and that its role declined in the 1990s once third-generation aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole (approved 1995) arrived; it also gives conflicting dates for US discontinuation [9]. A 1967 mechanism study and a 2026 history of early aromatase-inhibitor development both place aminoglutethimide at the start of that drug class [5][17]. Wikipedia describes it as now largely superseded by ketoconazole, abiraterone and newer aromatase inhibitors [1].

Lethargy is the most frequent effect (reported in 31 to 70 percent of patients) and the most common reason for stopping. Rash and low blood pressure each occur in about 15 percent, and at least one side effect occurs in 45 to 85 percent. Other effects include nausea, dizziness, depression, weight gain and liver toxicity. Severe toxicity occurs in about 10 percent, including circulatory collapse attributed to adrenal insufficiency, and bone marrow suppression is rare.[1]

It interacts with corticosteroids, warfarin and alcohol, and is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Labels and reviews call for monitoring of thyroid function, blood counts and liver enzymes.[1]
Aminoglutethimide is marketed in only a few countries, including China, Egypt and Lithuania, having formerly been sold in more than two dozen including the US, Canada and UK.[1]

Cytadren appears in bodybuilding lore around Austrian bodybuilder Andreas Munzer, who died on 14 March 1996 at age 31 after multiple organ failure. Wikipedia reports an autopsy finding of dystrophic multiple organ failure, with anabolic steroids, large amounts of potassium-sparing diuretics and traces of about 20 drugs described in a 2006 German dissertation; it does not name aminoglutethimide [15]. A T Nation thread says Cytadren abuse was one theory about his death, while a poster in another thread repeats a claim that too little cortisol can cause internal bleeding [11][12]. These are forum statements, not published findings.

In the sports context, a 2025 analysis of 601 seized samples from the illegal market found that about 35 percent of the post-cycle-therapy products tested lacked their declared active ingredient, and noted that such drugs are prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency; aminoglutethimide was not singled out [17]. Grokipedia says it is not a controlled substance in the US and that off-label bodybuilding use often involves illicit online sourcing [9].

Trials are in oncology and endocrinology. A randomised trial compared letrozole at two doses with aminoglutethimide in advanced breast cancer.[6] A completed phase 3 trial of tamoxifen with or without aminoglutethimide enrolled 2,021 postmenopausal women with early breast cancer, and a small phase 2 trial examined early medical adrenalectomy in prostate cancer.[7][8] Reviews trace its role as the first aromatase inhibitor.[2][3] No studies were found testing it for muscle, fat loss or other appearance goals. A 1981 Lancet editorial and Medical Letter piece reviewed the drug's profile when it was in clinical use [16][18].

lore.intro: On T Nation, Cytadren appears in estrogen-control and contest-prep discussions, alongside anastrozole and other agents.[10][13][14]

claims.claim: Cytadren works as an anti-aromatase for people on anabolic steroids.
claims.believers: Posters recommend it as an option for keeping estrogen down on testosterone-based stacks, alongside Arimidex.[14]
claims.experts: It lowers estradiol and aromatase activity in men and postmenopausal women in the medical literature, though it is described as a relatively weak inhibitor and causes lethargy in many patients.[1]

claims.claim: Cutting cortisol with Cytadren preserves muscle during contest prep.
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a cortisol suppressor, with one citing a doctor who found it beneficial to avoid cortisol inhibition at night while allowing some during the day.[13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says its usefulness for such purposes has been questioned; no trial has tested it for muscle or fat loss, and medical use pairs it with a corticosteroid to prevent adrenal insufficiency.[1][3]

claims.claim: Cytadren contributed to a famous bodybuilder's death.
claims.believers: A thread on Andreas Munzer says Cytadren abuse was one theory for his 1996 death.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports an autopsy giving dystrophic multiple organ failure, with steroids and diuretics discussed as contributors, and does not mention Cytadren [15]. The forum thread says no autopsy was performed; no published study links aminoglutethimide to his death.

claims.claim: Cytadren is too sedating to be worth using for physique goals
claims.believers: Posters say it is rarely worth the lethargy it causes and note that one trial showing an estrogen effect also gave hydrocortisone, which has independent benefits [13][14].
claims.experts: Lethargy is the most frequent side effect (31 to 70 percent of patients) and the most common reason for stopping treatment [1].

claims.claim: Because it blocks adrenal output it is a 'medical adrenalectomy' bodybuilders can borrow
claims.believers: Contest-prep discussions describe it as a cortisol suppressor [13].
claims.experts: Medicine uses the drug that way for Cushing's syndrome but pairs it with hydrocortisone to prevent adrenal insufficiency, and severe toxicity including circulatory collapse occurs in about 10 percent [1].

card.summary: An old adrenal-steroid and aromatase blocker with a rough side-effect profile; cortisol-cutting for physique is untested.
card.note: Common lethargy; adrenal insufficiency risk; requires corticosteroid cover in medical use.

quick.overview:
Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren) began as an epilepsy drug and was later used to treat Cushing's syndrome and hormone-sensitive cancers by blocking steroid production.

Some bodybuilders have used it to cut cortisol and control estrogen. Wikipedia notes that this use has been questioned and that few users report positive experiences. No trials have tested it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits several steroid-synthesis enzymes, notably P450scc in the adrenal gland and aromatase, lowering cortisol and estrogen.
quick.risks: Lethargy is the most common effect; rash, low blood pressure, liver toxicity and adrenal insufficiency are reported, and medical use pairs it with corticosteroid replacement. It is marketed in only a few countries.
